q-gi-verb.label: Which form the verb before it takes
q-gi-verb.summary: Enjoy, avoid, mind take -ing; want, hope, decide take to + verb; a few take either.

q-gi-prep.label: After a preposition or a fixed phrase
q-gi-prep.summary: Every preposition is followed by -ing, including the 'to' of look forward to and be used to.

q-gi-bare.label: Verbs followed by the bare verb
q-gi-bare.summary: Make, let, see, hear and had better take the verb with no 'to'.

q-gi-causative.label: Causative have / get + object + V3
q-gi-causative.summary: To say someone else did the work for you, 'have' and 'get' take the object followed by the past participle (V3), not the bare verb: had his hair cut, got the roof repaired.

rules.text: These take -ing: enjoy, avoid, mind, finish, stop, keep, suggest, recommend, consider, deny, admit, postpone, risk, practise, remember doing (= recall).
rules.bad: She avoided to answer the question.

rules.text: These take to + verb: want, hope, decide, agree, refuse, promise, manage, afford, intend, offer, fail, learn, remember to do (= not forget).
rules.ok: He refused to sign the form.

rules.text: A few verbs take either form but change meaning: 'stop smoking' means give it up, 'stop to smoke' means pause in order to smoke; 'remember posting' is a memory, 'remember to post' is a duty.
rules.ok: He stopped smoking last year. He stopped to smoke outside.
rules.bad: Treating the two as the same sentence.

rules.text: A preposition is always followed by -ing, never by a bare or to-form. This holds for phrases whose last word is 'to': look forward to, be used to, be accustomed to, object to, with a view to.
rules.ok: I look forward to meeting you. She is used to working nights.
rules.bad: I look forward to meet you. She is used to work nights.

rules.text: Make, let, see, hear, feel, watch and the phrases had better, would rather, rather than take the bare verb with no 'to'. In the passive, 'make' regains it: he was made to pay.
rules.ok: They made him pay. You had better go now.
rules.bad: They made him to pay. You had better to go now.

rules.text: To say that someone else did a job for you (rather than that you did it yourself), 'have' or 'get' takes the object followed by the past participle (V3), not the bare verb: had his hair cut, got the roof repaired. This differs from 'make', which names the doer and takes the bare verb (made him do the work).
rules.ok: She had her car washed yesterday.
rules.bad: She had her car wash yesterday.

q-gi-verb.cue: A blank after a verb such as enjoy, avoid, decide or refuse.
q-gi-verb.standard: Name the verb before the blank and recall which list it belongs to. If it takes either form, the meaning decides.
q-gi-verb.fast: Verbs about stopping, continuing and liking take -ing; verbs about intending and agreeing take 'to'.
q-gi-verb.eliminate: Drop the bare form at once unless the verb is make, let, see or hear.
traps: Avoid and suggest, which are often given 'to' by mistake.
Stop and remember, where the two forms mean different things.

q-gi-prep.cue: A blank after a preposition, or after look forward to, used to, accustomed to, object to.
q-gi-prep.standard: Check whether the word before the blank is a preposition. If it is, the answer is the -ing form.
q-gi-prep.fast: A 'to' that belongs to a fixed phrase still takes -ing.
q-gi-prep.eliminate: Remove the to-form and the bare form; only -ing can follow a preposition.
traps: 'Look forward to meet' and 'used to work', which read naturally and are wrong.
'Used to + bare verb' for a past habit is a different pattern: he used to walk.

q-gi-bare.cue: make, let, see, hear, had better or would rather before the blank.
q-gi-bare.standard: Use the bare verb. Add 'to' only when the sentence is passive with 'made'.
q-gi-bare.fast: No 'to' after make, let, see, hear, had better.
q-gi-bare.eliminate: Drop every option with 'to' unless the verb is in the passive.
traps: 'Made him to pay' and 'had better to go'.
The passive 'was made to pay', which does take 'to'.

q-gi-causative.cue: have/has/had or get/gets/got, followed by a thing (not a person) and a blank, meaning a job arranged rather than done personally.
q-gi-causative.standard: Check whether the subject did the job personally or had it done by someone else. If someone else did it, use the past participle (V3) after the object.
q-gi-causative.fast: had/got + thing + V3, not V1: had the car washed, not had the car wash.
q-gi-causative.eliminate: Drop the bare-verb option once the sentence clearly means a job done by someone else, not by the subject.
traps: Reading 'have/get' like 'make' and expecting the bare verb.
The object (hair, car, roof) is a thing, which is itself a clue that the subject is not doing the work personally.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
She avoided ___ the question twice.
practice.why: 'Avoid' belongs to the group that takes the -ing form.

a.note: 'Avoid to answer' applies the 'to' pattern to a verb that takes -ing.

d.note: 'To answering' puts a preposition and an -ing form together after a verb that needs neither.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
He refused ___ the receipt without a stamp.
practice.why: 'Refuse' belongs to the group that takes to + verb.

a.note: 'Refused signing' applies the -ing pattern to a verb that takes 'to'.

d.note: 'To signing' is not a possible combination here.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The committee suggested ___ the meeting to Friday.
practice.why: 'Suggest' takes the -ing form, or a that-clause with the base verb; it never takes 'to'.

a.note: 'Suggested to postpone' is one of the commonest errors of this kind.

c.note: A bare verb cannot follow 'suggested' without 'that'.

d.note: 'That postpone' has no subject in the clause.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
He stopped [[to smoke]] two years ago and his health improved.
practice.why: 'Stop smoking' means to give it up, which is what 'two years ago and his health improved' requires. 'Stop to smoke' would mean he paused in order to smoke.

b.note: 'Stopped to smoke' means he halted so that he could smoke, the opposite of giving it up.

c.note: 'To smoking' is not a possible form after 'stopped'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
I look forward to ___ from you soon.
practice.why: The 'to' of 'look forward to' is a preposition, so it takes the -ing form.

a.note: 'Look forward to hear' treats the 'to' as an infinitive marker; it is a preposition.

c.note: 'To have heard' puts a perfect infinitive after a preposition.

d.note: 'To be hearing' is not used in this fixed phrase.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
She is used to ___ in three languages every day.
practice.why: 'Be used to' means accustomed to, and its 'to' is a preposition, so the -ing form follows.

a.note: 'Used to work' with a bare verb means a past habit; the sentence here says she is accustomed to it.

c.note: A perfect infinitive cannot follow a preposition.

d.note: A past form cannot follow a preposition.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The residents objected / to pay the maintenance / until the lift / was repaired.
practice.why: 'Object to' takes the -ing form, so it should be 'to paying the maintenance'.

a.note: 'The residents objected' is a correct main clause.

c.note: 'Until the lift' correctly begins a clause of time.

d.note: 'Was repaired' is a correct passive verb for the lift.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The inspector made the driver ___ the papers at once.
practice.why: 'Make' takes the bare verb in the active voice.

a.note: 'Made him to produce' adds a 'to' that 'make' takes only in the passive.

c.note: An -ing form cannot follow 'made' in this pattern.

d.note: A past form cannot follow 'made' here.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
You had better ___ the doctor before the fever rises.

a.note: 'Had better to see' adds a 'to' the phrase never takes.

d.note: A past form cannot follow 'had better'.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
The clerk was [[made pay]] the difference out of his salary.
practice.why: In the passive, 'make' takes 'to': he was made to pay.

b.note: The bare verb is right in the active ('they made him pay') but the passive restores the 'to'.

c.note: An -ing form does not follow 'was made' in this sense.

d.note: 'Make' must agree with the past 'was' and cannot stay in the base form.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
She ___ her hair cut short before the interview.
practice.why: Causative 'had' + object + V3 says a job (the haircut) was done by someone else for her.

b.note: The present 'has' does not fit a sentence clearly set before a past event.

c.note: 'Had got' doubles the causative verb; only one is needed.

d.note: 'Had get' is not a grammatical form.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
We [[got repaired our roof]] before the monsoon arrived.
practice.why: The causative pattern is object + V3: got our roof repaired, not 'repaired our roof' or 'our roof repair'.

b.note: 'Got repair' is not a grammatical verb form here.

c.note: The object must be followed by the past participle 'repaired', not the bare verb 'repair'.

d.note: 'To repair' is not the pattern causative 'get' uses with an object.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The manager wants to / get the accounts audit / before the financial year / closes next month.
practice.why: Causative 'get' + object takes the past participle: 'get the accounts audited', not 'audit'.

a.note: 'The manager wants to' correctly begins the infinitive phrase.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
He is getting his old motorcycle ___ at the local garage.
practice.why: Causative 'get' + object takes the past participle: getting his motorcycle repaired.

a.note: The bare verb 'repair' follows 'make', not the causative 'get'.

c.note: 'To repair' is not the pattern this causative construction uses.

d.note: The -ing form describes an ongoing action by the subject, not a job arranged for someone else.
